The Von Neumann architecture is a computer model consisting of memory, a CPU, input devices, and output devices.
The Von Neumann bottleneck occurs when the shared memory limits how quickly the CPU can retrieve instructions and data.
A key advantage is flexibility: programs can be changed by changing the contents of memory.

The Von Neumann architecture consists of memory, a CPU, input devices, and output devices. Memory stores both instructions and data. Input devices provide data and instructions, while output devices present results. The CPU includes the Control Unit, which directs operations and decodes instructions, and the ALU, which performs arithmetic and logical operations. In the instruction cycle, the CPU fetches an instruction from memory, decodes it, executes it, and stores the result in memory or sends it to an output device.
